_about.one_line: Carry-free residue-number-system engine on ordinary CPUs: exact integer arithmetic on coprime prime rings, with a ternary pull engine, an exact training step and RNS modular exponentiation.
_about.licence: PolyForm Small Business 1.0.0 / PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 (LICENSING.md); PolyForm Free Trial for evaluation
_about.source: projects/outreach/claims-suite/claims.json rows C1 C2 C3 C4 C6 C7 C8 C9 (verified 2026-10-16); explanations from TECHNICAL-DISCLOSURE.md

tests.title: Carry-free T50 ring abacus: engine self-test 9/9
tests.claim: Carry-free T50 ring abacus (50 one-byte prime rings, 311-bit range): engine self-test 9/9
tests.verify: PYTHONPATH=engine python3 -m pytest -q engine/tests 2>&1 | tail -1 | grep -E 'passed'
tests.what_it_means: Nine unit tests load numbers into fifty prime rings (each one byte), add and multiply them ring by ring with no carries between rings, and rebuild the answer by the Chinese remainder theorem. Passing proves the ring arithmetic equals Python's exact big integers on every tested case inside the 311-bit range. It does not prove speed, and it does not cover division.
tests.how_we_got_it: Run `PYTHONPATH=engine python3 -m pytest -q engine/tests` on a laptop (Intel i5-8365U, Linux) on 2026-10-12; the pytest output is saved as experiments/pytest.2026-10-12.log. The same command re-runs it in about twenty seconds.
tests.use_in_your_work: Anywhere a sum or product must be exact and independent of the order it was computed in: ledgers that must balance to the unit, checksums over large integers, and any pipeline where two machines must reach the same integer answer.
tests.honest_limits: Division inside the rings is not implemented; the lattice multiplier (C4) is slower than GMP.

tests.title: Sign / ReLU decided from the rings without rebuilding the number
tests.claim: Sign / ReLU without rebuilding the number: 26,002 values, 0 wrong
tests.what_it_means: A residue number system hides the sign of a number: you normally have to convert the whole number back to read it. This probe reads the sign (and therefore a ReLU, max(0, x)) from the rings directly, and got all 26,002 test values right. Passing proves the sign rule is exact on that sample; it is a probe on random values, not a proof for every integer.
tests.how_we_got_it: experiments/probes.py, probe P1_sign_relu (50 rings, 311-bit range, 6,002 of the values placed at the edges near 0 and M/2); the result file experiments/probes.result.json holds the counts (values, wrong). `python3 experiments/probes.py` re-runs every probe in the file.
tests.use_in_your_work: Neural-network activations (ReLU) and comparisons on numbers kept in residue form, so a whole layer can stay in the rings between operations.
tests.honest_limits: Sampled, not exhaustive; the rule's range conditions are in TECHNICAL-DISCLOSURE.md.

tests.title: Bit-identical training step across 8 harnesses
tests.claim: Exact bit-identical training step across 8 harnesses (ternary, d=960): 0 forward/backward/dW mismatches
tests.what_it_means: One training step of a ternary (weights in {-1, 0, +1}) layer of width 960 was run on eight separate processes. In integer arithmetic every process produced the same forward activations, the same gradients and the same weight update, bit for bit. The same step in float32 differed in 118,026 of 921,600 entries of the latent between runs. Passing proves determinism of the integer path on this step; it does not say the integer step trains a better model, and it ran at 0.25x the float speed.
tests.how_we_got_it: experiments/tlut/train_step.py on an AVX-512 VBMI host, one core (the result file names it; 2026-10-12); eight harness processes hash their forward, backward and dW tensors and the result file records the mismatch counts. Re-run: `cd experiments/tlut && python3 train_step.py`.
tests.use_in_your_work: Training runs that must be reproducible across machines or auditable step by step (a receipt per step), and distributed training where every worker must agree exactly.
tests.honest_limits: Speed 108.0 vs 26.6 ms per step (0.25x float32); one layer, one width.

tests.title: Honest negative: Gelosia lattice core slower than GMP
tests.claim: Honest negative: Gelosia lattice core 4.5–16.9× slower than GMP at 2,000/8,000 bits
tests.what_it_means: This is a result where we lost. The lattice (Gelosia) big-number multiplier was benchmarked against GMP and is 4.5 to 16.9 times slower at 2,000 and 8,000 bits. It is kept in the suite so that the wins (C6, C7) are read next to the loss that led to them.
tests.how_we_got_it: experiments/bench_gelosia_kernel.py against gmpy2 on an AVX-512 host (native build) and on the AVX2 laptop; result files hold the per-size timings and ratios.
tests.use_in_your_work: If you need plain big-integer multiplication, use GMP. Use the rings when you need exactness across machines, carry-free parallelism, or the modular-exponentiation path (C6).

tests.title: Exact modular exponentiation faster than GMP's hardened powmod on one core
tests.claim: Exact modexp faster than GMP powmod_sec on one core: 2.07× at 2,048 bits, 2.96× at 4,096; 0 mismatches in 128 messages
tests.what_it_means: Modular exponentiation (the core of RSA, Diffie-Hellman and many proofs) was computed in residue rings of the form 2^48 - c, one residue per SIMD lane, eight messages at a time, with the same work per window so the exponent drives no branch. All 128 results equal GMP's; the run was 2.07x faster than GMP's side-channel-hardened powmod_sec at 2,048 bits and 2.96x at 4,096 bits on one core. This is a speed and exactness result, not a security claim: the code is not audited.
tests.how_we_got_it: experiments/gmp/bench_batch_ct.py (interleaved medians vs gmpy2) on an AVX-512 IFMA host; result file experiments/gmp/bench_batch_ct.result.json. Re-run needs gmpy2 and AVX-512 IFMA: `python3 experiments/gmp/bench_batch_ct.py`.
tests.use_in_your_work: Batch signing or verification servers, zero-knowledge and homomorphic-encryption kernels where many exponentiations share a modulus, and any place a carry-free exact big-number kernel maps onto SIMD lanes.
tests.honest_limits: No security audit; a Welch t-test on timings (0.37 / 0.40) is a leak check only. GMP is still faster at 1,024 bits.

tests.title: Fixed-base comb 7.8x at 2,048 bits
tests.what_it_means: When the base of the exponentiation is fixed (as in signing with one key), a precomputed comb table lets the rings answer 7.8 times faster than GMP at 2,048 bits, exact. The table costs memory and setup time, which the result file records.
tests.how_we_got_it: experiments/gmp/bench_comb.py on the same AVX-512 IFMA host as C6; result file experiments/gmp/bench_comb.result.json.
tests.use_in_your_work: Signing services and protocols that reuse one generator or key for many operations.
tests.honest_limits: Fixed base only; same no-security-claim as C6.

tests.title: BitNet b1.58 2B4T decoded on the Armilla pull: identical logits hash on three CPUs
tests.claim: BitNet b1.58 2B4T decoded on the Armilla pull: logits hash identical on i5-8365U and EPYC 4564P at 1/4/8 threads; Xeon 8481C (SPR) as the 3rd CPU: 16ba3979
tests.verify: test -s experiments/bitnet/README.md && echo 'see experiments/bitnet (model download + 3 CPUs needed)'
tests.expect: 1 distinct hash across threads and CPUs (16ba3979…)
tests.what_it_means: A public 2-billion-parameter ternary language model was decoded layer by layer through the ring pull engine on three different CPUs from two vendors, at one, four and eight threads, and every run produced the same SHA-256 of its logits. Passing proves the decode is bit-identical across machines and thread counts; at the fast path it ran 1.15x bitnet.cpp on the Xeon and 1.37x on the EPYC. It does not compare model quality with other inference engines beyond the perplexity rows in the disclosure.
tests.how_we_got_it: experiments/bitnet on the laptop (i5-8365U), an AMD EPYC 4564P and a Google Cloud Xeon Platinum 8481C (2026-10-15); thread-hash files per machine under experiments/bitnet/results/; the cross-machine comparison (GCP session 1, A1) ships with the claims kit's evidence folder and in the research corpus's status disclosure.
tests.use_in_your_work: Serving a local language model whose outputs can be checked by anyone with the same weights: reproducible evaluation, auditable inference, and CPU-only deployment without a GPU.
tests.honest_limits: Needs the model weights (about 1 GB) and hours of CPU to reproduce fully; marked external for that reason.
corrections: C08 wording: name the CPU with any per-element time

tests.title: 5-trit weight codes at 1.6 bits per weight
tests.claim: 5-trit weight codes at 1.6 bits/weight; pull 1.38× the 3-trit code and 1.51× bit-planes at 8192×7680, 0 mismatches (tie at 4096×3840)
tests.what_it_means: Five ternary weights packed into one byte (1.6 bits per weight) are pulled through a byte-permute lookup; at a large matrix the pull is 1.38x the 3-trit code and 1.51x a bit-plane layout, with zero mismatches against the plain computation. At the smaller size it is a tie, and the file says so.
tests.how_we_got_it: experiments/tlut/tlut5_bench.py on an AVX-512 VBMI host; result file experiments/tlut/tlut5_bench.result.json. Re-run: `python3 experiments/tlut/tlut5_bench.py` (needs VBMI).
tests.use_in_your_work: Smaller ternary model files and faster CPU matrix-vector pulls for local inference.
tests.honest_limits: Tie at 4096x3840; needs AVX-512 VBMI to re-run.
